**Solution 3 has the correct final answer, n₀ = 6, though its justification is partly wrong.**

**n = 4 fails.** The single edge V has δ₃ ≥ 1 but no Berge-C₄³, so n₀ ≥ 5.

**n = 5 fails.** Take the four 4-sets V∖{a}, V∖{b}, V∖{c}, V∖{d} on {a,b,c,d,e}. Every triple misses at least one of a,b,c,d, so δ₃ ≥ 1. The hypergraph has only 4 edges, so no Berge-C₅³ exists. Hence n₀ ≥ 6. Solution 3's specific construction (three 4-sets covering all 10 triples) is impossible, since any three 4-sets on 5 vertices leave the triple of their missing vertices uncovered. Its conclusion is still right.

**Solution 1 (answer 7) is wrong.** Its n = 6 counterexample is never actually constructed, and its Steiner-system argument for n = 7 is irrelevant. I checked the n = 6 case:
- **C₄ always exists for n ≥ 6.** For a 4-set Q that is not an edge, the four triples of Q have pairwise disjoint sets of covering edges, so Berge-C₄ on Q exists. If every 4-set is an edge, the triple T ⊂ Q can be matched to T ∪ {x} for distinct outside vertices x.
- **Extremal covers on 6 vertices have C₅ and C₆.** The only 6-edge cover with 4-sets is two disjoint triangles, and I found Berge-C₆ and Berge-C₅ in it. I also checked a wheel-type cover and a mixed 10-edge cover, and both contain C₆ (and C₅ for the mixed one).

This is not a full proof for n = 6, and I did not verify n ≥ 7 in general. But no counterexample on 6 vertices turned up, so n₀ = 6 is the best-supported value.

**Solution 2 (answer 3) is wrong.** Its own n = 4 counterexample shows the property fails at n = 4, so n₀ ≥ 5.

CHOICE: 3
